4. Hemovability and Administrative Adjudication. A persistent issue 
since the Court’s 2010 Free Enterprise Fund decision has been its implications 
for Administrative Law Judges, a group of agency adjudicators who enjoy 
statutory protection against at-will removal. Many ALJ s are employed by 
multi-member independent commissions that, unless Humphrey s Executor is 
overruled, continue also to enjoy statutory tenure protection. Congress created 
the position of independent ALJ’s (originally called “hearing officers ) in 
response to com pl aints by regulated parties about the potential for pro-
government bias among adjudicators on the payroll of the regulatory agencies 
prosecuting them. Applying to ALJ’s the Free Enterprise Fund prohibition 
against multi-tiered tenure protection would appear to render the institutional 
structure unconstitutional. In Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy, 
144 S. Ct. 2117 (2024), the Court sidestepped the question of whether the 
statutory protections afforded SEC ALJs are constitutional. The Court held, 
however, that where Congress creates statutory claims “whose causes of action 
are modeled on common lav/,” such suits must ordinarily be tried in Article III 
courts and not before an agency adjudicator. The rmphcations will be discussed 
in depth on Chapter 4 on Administrative Adjudication.
The Conundra of Vacancies
The Constitution’s default position for the appointment of officers of 
the United States divides the power between the President and the Senate. 
Not only are advice and consent required for all principal officers, but the 
Senate will be involved in the approval of inferior officers, as well, unless 
Congress, by statute, has made the affirmative decision to authorize 
another of the constitutionally preferred options. Continuity in 
government, however, creates the obvious problem that vacancies will 
occur that cannot be filled immediately by individuals nominated and 
confirmed for those precise positions.
Recess Appointments. The Constitution explicitly provides for one 
temporary fix, namely, recess appointments. Under Article II, § 2: “The 
President shall have Power to fill up all Vacancies that may happen during 
the Recess of the Senate, by granting Commissions which shall expire at 
the End of their next Session.” That option, however, does not fit all 
circumstances; for example, vacancies often occur when the Senate is not 
in recess. As a consequence, as early as 1795, Congress has also specified 
through statutes who may serve in an “acting” capacity during a hiatus 
between regularly confirmed (or even recess-appointed) incumbents.
Presidents have not been reluctant to use the recess appointment 
power. There were over 650 such appointments from the Reagan through
